about: CAPS-DI pedagogical knowledge base. CAPS says WHAT must be learned; these rules say HOW it is taught; learner data decides how teaching is adapted. Items marked origin=roadmap come from the CAPS-DI pedagogical roadmap; origin=added are common Foundation Phase errors added for coverage and should be reviewed.

barriers.name: Prerequisite gap
barriers.description: The learner does not know the skill yet.

barriers.name: Misconception
barriers.description: The learner has learned something incorrectly.

barriers.name: Access barrier
barriers.description: The learner may know the concept but cannot show it through the current mode of instruction.

barriers.name: Processing barrier
barriers.description: The learner needs more processing time, repetition or reduced cognitive load.

barriers.name: Language barrier
barriers.description: The learner understands the concept but lacks the vocabulary or English to express it.

barriers.name: Attention / regulation barrier
barriers.description: The learner cannot sustain engagement with the current instructional format.

barriers.name: Motor / transcription barrier
barriers.description: The learner knows what to write but handwriting limits output.

barriers.name: Insufficient challenge
barriers.description: The learner has already mastered the target and needs greater complexity.

dimensions.access: How learners take in the content: visuals, oral explanation, concrete materials, movement, audio, enlarged print, vocabulary pre-teaching.
dimensions.process: How learners work with the concept: extra modelling, reduced cognitive load, guided practice, repetition, structured partner work, manipulatives.
dimensions.support: Temporary scaffolds: prompts, cues, sentence frames, word banks, graphic organisers, worked examples, checklists.
dimensions.response: How learners show understanding: oral response, pointing, drawing, selecting, constructing, writing, reading aloud.
dimensions.challenge: How complexity rises for learners who have mastered the outcome: more complex text, independent application, explanation, justification, comparison, inference, creation.

phonics.name: Systematic explicit phonics
steps: Hear the sounds in the spoken word
Map each sound to its letter
Blend left to right and read the word
Then segment: break the word back into its sounds
Spell (encode) it, a letter for each sound
Apply in decodable text and dictation

oral.name: Oral language and vocabulary development
steps: Introduce words with pictures and objects

letterKnowledge.name: Multisensory letter introduction
steps: Trace it in sand or the air
Find it in words and the environment
Daily cumulative review of all letters taught

phonemic.name: Oral phonemic awareness (no print)
steps: Isolate sounds with counters or fingers
Swap a sound to make a new word
Then link the sounds to letters

segmenting.name: Segmenting for spelling (encoding)
steps: Tap or push a counter for each sound
Write a letter for each sound in order
Check by blending back what was written
Apply in dictated words and short sentences

Term 1.question: Does the learner have the foundational knowledge and skills for this CAPS outcome?
Term 1.sequence: Explicit teaching, modelling, guided practice, repetition, multisensory practice, immediate feedback
Term 1.look_for: prerequisite gaps, foundational misconceptions, language barriers, phonological difficulties, vocabulary gaps, attention or participation barriers

Term 2.question: Can the learner use foundational skills to understand and communicate meaning?
Term 2.sequence: Model, guided practice, purposeful practice, feedback, application
Term 2.look_for: whether the difficulty is decoding or meaning (vocabulary, comprehension) — respond to the actual barrier, not with more of the same

Term 3.question: What is preventing this learner from accessing the same CAPS outcome?
Term 3.sequence: Diagnose the barrier from evidence, then adapt access, process, support, response or challenge
Term 3.look_for: the specific barrier type (prerequisite, misconception, access, processing, language, attention, motor, insufficient challenge)

Term 4.question: Can the learner apply the skill independently in a new context?
Term 4.sequence: Model, guide, prompt, fade, independent application, transfer
Term 4.look_for: self-correction, strategy choice, explaining thinking, applying the skill to unfamiliar texts and tasks, readiness for the next grade

misconceptions.misconception: Confuses visually similar letters
misconceptions.evidence: Reads or writes b for d, p for q
misconceptions.response: Multisensory formation with verbal path; one letter at a time; anchor picture or gesture for each

misconceptions.misconception: Does not yet recognise the taught letters
misconceptions.evidence: Cannot point to or name letters that have been taught
misconceptions.response: Multisensory letter introduction (shape, sound, formation) with daily cumulative review

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot separate the sounds in a word
misconceptions.evidence: Gives syllables instead of individual sounds
misconceptions.response: Oral phoneme segmentation before print (sound boxes, counters, tapping)

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot hear the first sound in a spoken word
misconceptions.evidence: Cannot say which of 'mat, sun, map' start the same way
misconceptions.response: Oral sound isolation games with no print: 'I spy something starting with /m/'; mouth-shape mirrors

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot blend sounds they hear
misconceptions.evidence: Teacher says /s/-/u/-/n/ and the learner cannot say 'sun'
misconceptions.response: Oral blending before print: stretch the sounds ('sssuuunnn'), robot talk, start with two sounds

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks the letter name is the sound
misconceptions.evidence: Says the letter name (e.g. 'em') instead of the sound /m/
misconceptions.response: Explicit sound discrimination and grapheme–phoneme mapping

misconceptions.misconception: Relies on memorised words instead of decoding
misconceptions.evidence: Reads familiar words but cannot read unfamiliar CVC words
misconceptions.response: Hear, segment, map sounds to letters, blend, read, encode, apply in text

misconceptions.misconception: Reads from the first letter only
misconceptions.evidence: Guesses words that start with the same sound
misconceptions.response: Segment every phoneme, then blend all the way through the word

misconceptions.misconception: Says each sound but cannot blend them into a word
misconceptions.evidence: Reads /c/ /a/ /t/ correctly but does not say 'cat'
misconceptions.response: Continuous blending: hold each sound into the next; start with stretchy sounds (m, s, a); successive blending (ca… cat)

misconceptions.misconception: Blends out of order
misconceptions.evidence: Reads 'tac' or 'act' for cat
misconceptions.response: Finger-track left to right; sweep under the word; sound boxes with arrows

misconceptions.misconception: Hears only the first sound of a word
misconceptions.evidence: Asked for the sounds in 'cat', says /c/ and stops; spells cat as 'c' or 'k'
misconceptions.response: Sound boxes with counters: push one counter per sound; stretch the word slowly ('mmmaaat')

misconceptions.misconception: Splits words into chunks, not single sounds
misconceptions.evidence: Says 'c – at' instead of /c/ /a/ /t/
misconceptions.response: Model one sound per finger or counter; contrast chunk vs sound; practise with two- then three-sound words

misconceptions.misconception: Hears the sounds but writes them in the wrong order
misconceptions.evidence: Writes 'tac' or 'cta' for cat
misconceptions.response: Say-tap-write: tap each sound left to right on the arm or sound boxes, then write each letter in that order; blend back to check

misconceptions.misconception: Guesses words from the pictures
misconceptions.evidence: Correct only when the picture supports the word
misconceptions.response: Cover picture cues; decode first, then confirm meaning with the picture

misconceptions.misconception: Reads word by word
misconceptions.evidence: Accurate but slow, laboured reading without phrasing
misconceptions.response: Model phrasing; repeated, meaningful rereading; echo and choral reading

misconceptions.misconception: Retells isolated events
misconceptions.evidence: Cannot say what the story is mostly about
misconceptions.response: Sequencing with picture cards and modelling of the main idea

misconceptions.misconception: Answers literal but not inferential questions
misconceptions.evidence: Performance drops when the question asks why or what might happen
misconceptions.response: Explicit inference modelling and graduated questioning (literal to inferential)

misconceptions.misconception: Decodes accurately but does not attend to meaning
misconceptions.evidence: Reads the text correctly but cannot answer simple questions about it
misconceptions.response: Pre-teach key vocabulary; stop and talk about meaning; oral retell after each page

misconceptions.misconception: Gives answers not supported by the text
misconceptions.evidence: Cannot point to what in the text or picture shows the answer
misconceptions.response: Ask 'What makes you think that?'; model finding evidence

misconceptions.misconception: Follows only part of an instruction
misconceptions.evidence: Completes the first step of a two-step instruction only
misconceptions.response: Chunk instructions; visual cue cards; learner repeats the steps back before starting

misconceptions.misconception: Answers in single words
misconceptions.evidence: Gives one-word answers even when prompted for more
misconceptions.response: Model full-sentence answers; sentence frames; think-pair-share oral rehearsal

misconceptions.misconception: Retells events out of order
misconceptions.evidence: Mixes the beginning, middle and end when retelling
misconceptions.response: Picture sequencing cards; first, then, last frames; act out the story

misconceptions.misconception: Uses broad, general words
misconceptions.evidence: Says 'thing', 'nice', 'big' instead of precise words
misconceptions.response: Explicit vocabulary instruction with pictures and objects; build word webs

misconceptions.misconception: Writes ideas as disconnected sentences
misconceptions.evidence: Sentences do not link to one another
misconceptions.response: Oral rehearsal, sentence combining and sequencing

misconceptions.misconception: Does not mark sentence boundaries
misconceptions.evidence: Writing has no capital letters or full stops
misconceptions.response: Model and orally 'say the sentence'; capital-and-full-stop checklist; shared editing

misconceptions.misconception: Leaves out vowels when spelling
misconceptions.evidence: Writes 'ct' for cat, 'dg' for dog
misconceptions.response: Oral segmenting with sound boxes before writing; vowel focus with anchor pictures

misconceptions.misconception: Writes exactly as they speak
misconceptions.evidence: The same sentence errors recur in writing
misconceptions.response: Explicit sentence modelling and guided transformation

misconceptions.misconception: Knows the letter but forms it inconsistently
misconceptions.evidence: Letters start in the wrong place or vary in size
misconceptions.response: Multisensory formation practice and reduced copying load

misconceptions.misconception: Copies letter by letter from the board
misconceptions.evidence: Very slow copying, loses place, incomplete work
misconceptions.response: Copy from a card on the desk; copy whole words; reduce copying length

misconceptions.misconception: Has already mastered the outcome
misconceptions.evidence: Completes tasks quickly and accurately; disengages
misconceptions.response: Increase complexity: explain, justify, apply to a new text, create

misconceptions.misconception: Cannot sustain attention in long whole-class input
misconceptions.evidence: Off task after a few minutes; better in short, active tasks
misconceptions.response: 3–5 minute segments, movement breaks, active response (cards, gestures)

decoding.note: Decoding and encoding have five components, taught in this order: letter knowledge, phonemic awareness, alphabetic principle, blending, then segmenting. Diagnose which one breaks down; each needs a different response.

components.name: Letter knowledge
components.what: Recognises the shapes and names of letters and letter combinations

components.name: Phonemic awareness
components.what: Purely auditory: hears, isolates, blends, segments and swaps individual sounds in spoken words — no print

components.name: Alphabetic principle
components.what: Knows that letters (graphemes) map systematically to sounds (phonemes)

components.name: Blending
components.what: Says the sounds left to right and smooths them into a word (reading)

components.name: Segmenting
components.what: The reverse of blending: breaks a spoken word into all its separate sounds and writes a letter for each sound (spelling / encoding)
